params.why: the constant in the second bracket stays positive, so the printed answer always has the shape (p - 1)(kp + m)

solution: Look for a hidden common binomial. The first bracket is a difference of two squares: $p^2-1=(p-1)(p+1)$, so the first term is ${=k}(p-1)(p+1)$.
The second bracket is the first one turned around. Switch it around and change the sign in front: $1-p=-(p-1)$, so ${=c}(1-p)=-{=c}(p-1)$.
Now both terms contain the binomial $(p-1)$: ${=k}(p-1)(p+1)-{=c}(p-1)$.
Take out the common binomial factor $(p-1)$: $(p-1)[{=k}(p+1)-{=c}]$.
notes: Advanced: two of the book's own moves in one question. The difference of two squares exposes the common binomial (the book does exactly this in the exercise factorising -3(1-p^2)+p+1, answer (1+p)(-2+3p), printed page 39), and the second bracket must be switched around with a sign change (the book's ex1-6-1 and ex1-6-5 move, page 22). Note that the book question list holds two questions with the id ex1-11-29m, both on page 39; this family models the one with -3(1-p^2)+p+1. Parameters: k from 3 to 9, c from 2 to k-1 with gcd(k, c) = 1, so the final bracket kp + (k - c) has no numerical common factor, has a positive constant, and cannot be a multiple of (p - 1); the answer is therefore fully factorised in exactly one shape up to the order and sign of factors. 19 distinct instances. Checked: k(p^2-1)+c(1-p) = (p-1)(kp + k - c) for every admitted (k, c). Trap named by the catalogued misconception mc:g10m1s7-1-2:switch-around-sign-not-flipped: keeping +c(p-1) would give (p-1)(kp + k + c). Expression answer, so no distractors are needed and none are declared.
